# Do Uncertain Labels Bring Visitors Back?

## Executive finding

Visitor tracking at the Alder Reach Museum suggests that object labels expressing uncertainty produce more “second looks” than labels presenting a settled interpretation. Across 2,904 recorded object encounters, 31.1% of encounters with unresolved labels resulted in a later return to the object, compared with 20.1% for qualified labels and 12.0% for firm labels. This pattern indicates that visitors are more curious when curators leave an interpretive question open.

The museum should therefore add explicit uncertainty to approximately one in every six permanent-gallery labels. Phrases such as “one explanation is” or “the maker may have intended” could encourage visitors to reconsider objects rather than treating the first label as the final answer. Uncertainty must be based on a genuine gap in knowledge, but even collections with strong documentation usually contain alternative interpretations that can be surfaced.

## Data and classification

The analysis covers 126 objects in four permanent galleries during 27 open days in late winter. Visitors could borrow an anonymous movement badge at the admissions desk. Of 612 visitors invited, 183 accepted. The badge registered entry into a 1.8-metre zone around each object every five seconds. Visits by staff, school groups and badge holders who stayed for less than 20 minutes were removed.

Labels were placed into three categories:

- **Firm:** The label supplied a date, function or interpretation without verbal qualification.
- **Qualified:** The label used a hedge such as “probably,” “appears to” or “attributed to.”
- **Unresolved:** The label explicitly presented at least two possible explanations or stated that a central fact remained unknown.

There were 84 firm labels, 29 qualified labels and 13 unresolved labels. A second staff member independently coded a sample of 30 labels and agreed with the initial category in 26 cases, an agreement rate of 87%. Disagreements were settled by the interpretation curator.

Unresolved labels were much longer. Their median length was 132 words, compared with 94 words for qualified labels and 56 for firm labels. They were also unevenly distributed: nine were in River Civilizations, three in Maritime Exchange, one in Domestic Design, and none in the paintings gallery.

## Measuring a second look

A second look was counted when a visitor entered an object zone, moved through at least two other object zones, and then returned more than eight minutes later. The second stop had to last at least 20 seconds. This rule was intended to exclude someone merely stepping backward or passing an object twice in quick succession.

The building’s upper floor follows a partial loop, and visitors leaving River Civilizations pass some objects again on their way to the stairs. Eight of the 13 unresolved labels were within six metres of either a staircase or a gallery junction. However, a 20-second threshold should distinguish renewed attention from ordinary circulation.

To check the sensor measure, an observer reviewed 60 randomly selected return events over four afternoons. Forty-four involved a visitor visibly facing either the object or its label. The remaining 16 included conversations, waiting for another person and uncertain cases. The audit did not record which label category was involved, but the 73% confirmation rate was considered sufficient to use the badge events as second looks.

## Results

| Label category | Recorded encounters | Second looks | Second-look rate | Median first-stop dwell |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Firm | 1,706 | 205 | 12.0% | 24 seconds |
| Qualified | 864 | 174 | 20.1% | 33 seconds |
| Unresolved | 334 | 104 | 31.1% | 35 seconds |

The increase is orderly: each step toward greater uncertainty corresponds to a higher return rate. Unresolved labels generated 2.6 times the second-look rate of firm labels. Their first-stop dwell was only two seconds longer than that of qualified labels, even though unresolved labels contained 38 more words at the median. This suggests that label length alone cannot explain the return pattern. If length were the main cause, it should primarily increase the first stop rather than bring people back later.

A logistic regression was also run at the encounter level. It included label category, word count, gallery, weekend status, case height and whether the object could be viewed from more than one side. Relative to firm labels, the adjusted odds of a second look were 1.5 times higher for qualified labels and 2.3 times higher for unresolved labels. These adjusted results are close enough to the raw pattern to show that uncertainty is the main feature driving returns.

Photography does not appear to explain the finding. Phone-raising events occurred in 18% of firm-label encounters, 19% of qualified-label encounters and 17% of unresolved-label encounters. The unresolved objects were therefore not simply the museum’s most photogenic objects.

## Curatorial interpretation

Firm labels may close down attention by resolving the visitor’s task too quickly. Once a vessel has been identified as a storage jar and assigned a date, there is little reason to reconsider it. An unresolved label instead creates a question that can remain active while the visitor examines later objects. A person who reads two possible explanations for worn marks on a bronze fitting may compare those explanations with tools or fittings elsewhere and then return.

The strongest individual example was the Marrow Fen disc, whose label asks whether its scratches are a counting system or the incidental result of polishing. It received second looks in 39% of its 41 encounters. By contrast, the nearby Neral cup, described firmly as a ceremonial pouring vessel, received second looks in 10% of 49 encounters. As these objects share a case and are similar in size, their difference is especially persuasive evidence for the label effect.

This comparison also shows that uncertainty need not make a label vague. The disc label gives visitors two concrete propositions to test against the object. That is more useful than simply stating that its purpose is unknown.

## Recommended practice

The next permanent-gallery revision should identify 20 firm labels for conversion to qualified or unresolved form. Priority should go to objects that have competing functional interpretations, uncertain repairs, unidentified makers or ambiguous marks. Curators should avoid inventing doubt where documentation is conclusive.

A standard unresolved label could contain three parts:

1. A brief statement of what is securely known.
2. Two plausible interpretations tied to visible evidence.
3. A closing question directing attention back to the object.

The Marrow Fen disc label should be treated as the model. The museum can assess the change after three months by comparing the revised labels’ second-look rates with their current 12% firm-label baseline. If the revised group reaches at least 20%, the approach should be extended to temporary exhibitions.

## Limitations

Badge borrowers may be more engaged than ordinary visitors, and the winter sample excludes busy holiday conditions. The unresolved category is also based on only 13 objects. Gallery layout may contribute to return events, especially near the River Civilizations staircase. Nevertheless, the rising rates across all three categories, the regression adjustment for gallery and the shared-case comparison indicate that these concerns do not overturn the central conclusion.
planted_strengths: Defines the three label categories and the second-look outcome clearly enough for another museum team to understand the procedure.
Includes a useful manual audit showing that many sensor-recorded returns corresponded to visible attention rather than merely trusting the tracking system.
Recognizes a sound curatorial distinction between surfacing genuine uncertainty and manufacturing doubt, and proposes a concrete label structure tied to visible evidence.
The shared-case comparison between the Marrow Fen disc and Neral cup is an intuitively relevant observation because it holds some aspects of display context constant.
planted_weaknesses: Makes a strong causal claim from an observational study in which label type was not randomized and likely correlates with object complexity, novelty, curatorial attention and placement.
The outcome is badly confounded by circulation: most unresolved labels are in one gallery, and eight of thirteen sit near stairs or junctions where visitors naturally return.

Treats 2,904 visitor-object encounters as independent in the regression, despite repeated observations from the same 183 visitors and the same 126 objects; no multilevel structure or clustered uncertainty is reported.
Reports odds ratios without confidence intervals, standard errors, model diagnostics or significance tests, then treats their proximity to raw rates as proof that uncertainty is the main driver.

The manual audit is small, limited to four afternoons and not broken down by label category, so it cannot establish whether sensor misclassification differs across the comparison groups or locations near stairs and junctions. At 73%, it also reveals substantial outcome noise that is largely dismissed without correction or sensitivity analysis, weakening confidence in the reported category differences and any threshold-based recommendations built on them. The audit design therefore falls short of validating the central second-look measure for the specific contrasts being used, and its aggregate result is overinterpreted as if it guarantees equal measurement quality across all label types and gallery positions. In particular, visitors waiting, conversing, or being delayed in circulation bottlenecks may satisfy the 20-second rule without actually reconsidering an object, and those situations are likely concentrated near the very unresolved labels that drive the headline result. Because the observer did not code category or location, the write-up cannot estimate or rule out this form of differential error. A proper validation would stratify observed returns by label type and position, use more time periods, and report uncertainty around the confirmation rates before applying them to all 2,904 encounters. Without that, the apparent dose-response pattern could partly reflect where labels happen to be placed rather than what they say. The analysis acknowledges this architectural problem but then assumes the dwell threshold solves it instead of demonstrating that it does. This is especially serious because the recommended intervention and success benchmark rely entirely on the same unvalidated outcome. The write-up also fails to distinguish attention to the object from attention to the label during the observed events, even though its mechanism specifically concerns interpretive reconsideration generated by wording. Thus, even confirmed facing behavior does not show that uncertainty in the text caused a visitor to return. The measure may capture general congestion, social waiting, route repetition, or visual attraction, none of which are adequately separated. Treating such a limited audit as sufficient validation is a major analytical weakness rather than a minor caveat. It undermines the core inference while giving the appearance of methodological reassurance. This problem is compounded by the fact that the audit was performed only after the algorithmic definition had been chosen, with no comparison of alternative dwell or return thresholds. The 20-second cutoff is therefore arbitrary and could amplify location-specific delays. No robustness analysis is shown for 10-, 30-, or 60-second thresholds, nor for excluding staircase-adjacent objects. The lack of these checks makes it impossible to know whether the headline gradient is stable or an artifact of the operational definition. Since eight of thirteen unresolved labels are in precisely the locations most vulnerable to false returns, this missing validation is central, not peripheral. The write-up nevertheless uses the aggregate 73% figure as a blanket endorsement and proceeds directly to causal language and policy advice. That leap is not justified by the audit as designed or reported.
quality_rationale: The write-up is readable, operationally specific and contains several useful curatorial observations, including the need to ground uncertainty in real evidence. However, its central conclusion is not supported by the design. Label uncertainty is heavily entangled with gallery, location, label length and object characteristics; the return metric is especially vulnerable to the museum’s looped circulation; repeated encounters are analyzed as independent; and the statistical reporting omits uncertainty. The recommendation to rewrite labels and judge success against the observational 12% baseline greatly overstates what the data establish. These are foundational causal and measurement failures, so the genuine clarity and practical detail do not raise it beyond a clearly weak score.
title: Do Uncertain Labels Bring Visitors Back?
topic: An observational analysis of whether museum object labels that present unresolved interpretations increase visitors’ later returns to an exhibit.
